Chapter 10, Vibhūtiyoga, "the yoga of the divine manifestations," has Kṛṣṇa resume his teaching once more for Arjuna's benefit, opening by restating his own unoriginated nature — without beginning among gods or great sages, the one source from whom they all spring — and by cataloging the many states of mind (intellect, knowledge, patience, truth, fear, fearlessness, non-violence, and more) that arise from him alone, before naming the seven great sages and the four Manus, ancestors of all beings, as likewise born of his mind and his power. Whoever truly knows this unoriginated greatness, Kṛṣṇa says, is freed from delusion and worshipped by the wise with a devotion that grants understanding itself. Arjuna responds with an extended eulogy, affirming Kṛṣṇa as the supreme brahman, the supreme abode, the eternal divine Person, praised as such by the sages and by Kṛṣṇa's own testimony, and then presses him, since only Kṛṣṇa can truly know himself, to declare without remainder the full extent of his own divine manifestations and his yoga, insisting he can never tire of hearing it. Kṛṣṇa agrees, conceding only that the chief manifestations can be told since his extent has no end, and unfolds the poem's great catalog (vv.19-39): he is the Self seated in the heart of all beings, the beginning, middle and end of all; and then, class by class, he identifies himself as the foremost of each — Viṣṇu among the Ādityas, the sun among lights, Indra among gods, Śiva among the Rudras, Meru among mountains, the ocean among bodies of water, Bhṛgu among sages, the sacred syllable Oṃ among utterances, the Himālaya, the sacred fig tree, Nārada, Uccaiḥśravas and Airāvata born of the churning of the ocean, the wish-fulfilling cow, the serpent Ananta, Varuṇa, Yama, Prahlāda, Time itself, the lion, Garuḍa, the wind, Rāma, the crocodile, the Gaṅgā, the science of the individual self, debate, the syllable A, the copulative compound, the great feminine qualities of fame, fortune, speech, memory, intelligence, steadfastness and patience, sacred chants and metres and months and seasons, gambling, splendor, victory, resolve, virtue, his own clan-name Vāsudeva, Arjuna himself among the Pāṇḍavas, Vyāsa among sages, Uśanas among poets, the rod of the punisher, the policy of the ambitious, the silence of secrets, and the knowledge of the knowing, before declaring that he is simply the seed of all beings, and that nothing whatsoever, moving or unmoving, could exist without him. The chapter closes (vv.40-42) by insisting the catalog is inexhaustible, offered only as a sample of his extent, and that whatever being anywhere possesses glory, splendor or vigor has sprung from a mere fraction of Kṛṣṇa's own splendor — so that, he tells Arjuna, all this detailed enumeration hardly matters next to the one plain fact: he stands sustaining the entire universe with but a single fraction of himself.
